summary: Summarizes a 1990 workshop at Harvard's Kennedy School on the commercialization of the Internet and the policy questions it raised. It is an informational report of discussions, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A group of experts met to talk about what happens when businesses start using the Internet. This is their meeting report.

subtitle: A 1990 workshop report on commercializing Internet infrastructure

tldr.problem: The Internet was built with government funding and restricted to research and education. As it grew, questions arose about whether and how commercial users and companies should be allowed to use and operate it.
tldr.mechanism: A 1990 workshop at Harvard brought together experts to discuss commercialization (allowing commercial users and providers) versus privatization (removing government role), and how to shift subsidies from the backbone to users or regions.
tldr.outcome: The report outlines policy options but makes no recommendations. It documents the tensions between academic control, market efficiency, and universal access that shaped the Internet's evolution.

today: RFC 1192 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It documents thinking about Internet commercialization at a pivotal moment in 1990, before the World Wide Web, before widespread commercial Internet access, and before email became dominant. The issues raised—who should fund the backbone, how to balance public access with private investment, how to manage growth—remained central to Internet policy for years after.

sections.title: The Commercialization Question
sections.content:
In 1990, the Internet was already partially commercial. Companies had mail gateways to commercial services like MCIMAIL and Compuserve. Performance Systems International (PSI) and UUNET marketed TCP/IP services. RLG sold database access over the Internet. But the NSFNET backbone, which connected most of the network, was a free resource available only to researchers and educators. Commercial use had to pass tests about whether it served research and education.

This RFC reports on a March 1990 workshop where experts debated two linked questions: should commercialization be allowed at all? And should the government still pay for the backbone? Workshop director Stephen Wolff distinguished commercialization (allowing commercial users and providers on the network) from privatization (removing government subsidy and control).
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet was like a public library built with tax money. Some businesses wanted to use it. People debated whether that was fair, and whether the government should keep running it.

sections.title: Privatization in Practice
sections.content:
By 1990, the Internet was already substantially privatized in some ways. Private companies owned the physical circuits, and private firms managed and operated most logical networks. The nonprofit regional networks contracted out routine operations to the private sector while keeping policy control. At the federal level, NSF contributed less than 3 million dollars of the NSFNET backbone's 10 million dollar annual cost; the rest came from Michigan, IBM, and MCI.

At the regional level, NSF funded about 40 percent of operating costs. Campus networks, though not federally funded, were much larger investments than the backbone or regional networks. The full Internet was thus a mixed system of public subsidy and private operation, not purely government-funded.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet was already mostly run by private companies, just paid for by the government. So it was not clear what privatization really meant.

sections.title: The Backbone as a Subsidized Good
sections.content:
The NSFNET backbone was provided free to all authorized networks. This subsidy encouraged usage but discouraged private investment in competing backbone networks. It constrained the market for commercial TCP/IP services by offering an established and growing user base a subsidized alternative to commercial providers.

The workshop considered four options: shift the subsidy to researchers (through grants), to institutions (through direct funding), to regional networks (by charging them for backbone access), or to service providers. Each option had advantages and drawbacks. Funding researchers could segregate the user community. Funding institutions risked entitlement program complexity. Funding regional networks would level the playing field but raise their costs. Each path involved trade-offs between market efficiency, universal access, and administrative simplicity.
sections.plainLanguage: Free Internet backbone for researchers is good if you want everyone to have access, but bad for private companies trying to sell their own backbone services.

sections.title: The National Research and Education Network
sections.content:
The high-bandwidth National Research and Education Network (NREN) was proposed to eventually replace the NSFNET. The NREN would serve research and education, but also had the potential to serve education at all levels, medical services, and public libraries. Broadening the purpose made it harder to define eligible users and easier to argue for limiting scope.

The report presented the evolution from discipline-specific networks (for physics or computer science research) to national infrastructure serving broad social needs. It suggested that pricing would eventually become more sophisticated, with usage-based charges for high-bandwidth services like videoconferencing. The vision was an aggregation of specialized resources in a common, negotiable environment.
sections.plainLanguage: The new NREN would be even bigger and serve more types of users. But that made it harder to decide who should pay for it.

sections.title: Policy Alternatives
sections.content:
The workshop discussed an alternative approach: NSF could bar mature services like email and news from the backbone, forcing private providers to offer their own mail backbone. This would reduce backbone traffic by about 30 percent and encourage innovation in commercial services. But it would be politically difficult (NSF had traditionally left regional networks autonomous) and would hurt regional networks financially by removing a service that attracted members.

The report notes that no regional network had yet failed from higher prices, but concerns about viability suggested any subsidy withdrawal should proceed in phases. The backbone could become a nonprofit or for-profit utility, each with different incentives and consequences for competition with private carriers.
sections.plainLanguage: One idea was to ban email from the free backbone to make room for private companies to sell better email service. But that might hurt smaller networks.
